exercise.name: Hanging Oblique Knee Raise
aliases: Hanging knee raise to the side

reference.title: Hanging Oblique Knee Raise
reference.listing: Video (movement reference; the page could not be read at authoring time, so the movement is taken from the exercise name and standard coaching practice)
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

exercise.mechanics: Compound (hip and knee flexion with trunk rotation and side bend, hanging)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as the knees rise to the side, in on the way down.
breathing.cadence: About 1.2 s up, 1.5 s down per side

prescription.tempo: About 1.2 s up, brief hold, 1.5 s down
prescription.progression: Higher knees, slower lowering, then straight legs to the side

cues.text: Hang from the bar, hands about shoulder width, legs together.
Draw the knees up and across toward the right elbow; the pelvis turns and the right side shortens.
Lower slowly to the centre hang without swinging.
Now up and across to the left side.
Lower slowly and settle the hang.

mistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs side to side
mistakes.fix: Lower to a still centre hang before each rep.

mistakes.mistake: Only turning the legs (no trunk work)
mistakes.fix: Lift the hip toward the ribs on the working side.
Keep the shoulder blades set down.

kinematics.norm: Knees to about hip height or higher, about 90-110 degrees (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: ≈-29° toward the working side; spine counter-rotates 31° so the shoulders stay square
kinematics.norm: Pelvis turns about 20-30 degrees toward the working side (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: Working side shortens (pelvis roll -12°, spine side bend 15°)
kinematics.norm: The working side shortens: hip toward the ribs (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: Per side: 1.2 s up, 0.4 s hold, 1.6 s down, 0.5 s still hang
kinematics.norm: About 1.2 s up and 1.5 s down per side (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual 5136, Hanging Oblique Knee Raise, video (movement reference)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
Escamilla et al. 2006, electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises (Phys Ther 86(5):656-671)
Oliva-Lozano and Muyor 2020, core muscle activity during physical fitness exercises: a systematic review (Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(12):4306)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Check the bar is secure and can take your weight before hanging from it.
Shoulder pain in the hang: shorten the set or use arm straps.
Low back pain: keep the twist small and avoid swinging; combined flexion and twisting under load is a common irritant.
modify: Grip gives out first: use arm straps.

muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris lift the legs from the hang.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris lift the legs from the hang.
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the pelvis up and controls the swing; hanging raises rank among the hardest abdominal exercises (Axler and McGill 1997).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External oblique on the left and internal oblique on the right turn and side-bend the pelvis toward the right knee drive (and the reverse for the left).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Mirror of the right side: they drive the knees toward the left.
muscleNotes.forearm_flexors_r: Grip the bar for the whole set.
muscleNotes.forearm_flexors_l: Grip the bar for the whole set.
muscleNotes.lats_r: Keep the shoulders set and the arms pulling slightly down on the bar.
muscleNotes.lats_l: Keep the shoulders set and the arms pulling slightly down on the bar.
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Steady the shoulder blade in the overhead hang.
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Steady the shoulder blade in the overhead hang.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Rectus femoris helps flex the hip.
muscleNotes.quads_l: Rectus femoris helps flex the hip.
